clue.text: Game's square between yellows and greens in London?

definitions.text: Game's square between yellows and greens in London?

parts.words: Game's square between yellows and greens in London?
parts.note: on the London Monopoly board the corner square sits between the yellow property set and the green set

explanation.walkthrough: Monopoly, the property board game, has its London streets in colour groups; the corner square between the yellows (Leicester Square, Coventry Street, Piccadilly) and the greens (Regent Street, Oxford Street, Bond Street) sends a player to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the instruction printed on that Monopoly corner square, ordering the player off to prison.

clue.text: Grand, large stove in farmhouse

parts.note: a range is a large cooking stove

explanation.surface: A grand, big stove sits in a country farmhouse kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A grange is a farmhouse with its outbuildings, the word's standard British sense.

clue.text: Cutting a new cloth

parts.note: a cutting remark is tart, sharp and biting

explanation.surface: Someone is cutting out a fresh piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' looks like scissors at work on the cloth, but here it is an adjective, as in a cutting remark.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartan is a woollen fabric woven in a pattern of crossing coloured stripes, especially Scottish clan checks.

clue.text: Salt on fish for nursery rhyme character

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another comes first, above it

parts.note: a salt is an old sailor, as is a jack (jack tar)
a sprat is a small sea fish

explanation.surface: Salt sprinkled on a fish, all for a character from a children's rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' reads as seasoning, but it means a sailor, and a jack is a sailor too.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Sprat is the man in the old rhyme who could eat no fat.

clue.text: With child, tribe inside creating an obstruction

indicators.note: the word for tribe goes within the phrase for obstructing

parts.note: something obstructing is in the way
a tribe is a family or clan

explanation.surface: Someone with a child and a whole tribe in tow is blocking the path.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a colloquial way of saying a woman is pregnant, carrying a baby.

clue.text: Paintings in health club in ancient city

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the word for paintings sits within the health club

parts.note: a spa is a health club or resort
paintings collectively are art

explanation.surface: Pictures hang in a gym or spa in some old Greek city.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has two 'in's: the first puts one piece inside the other, the second is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparta was a powerful city-state of ancient Greece, rival of Athens.

clue.text: Boy skipped round houses

indicators.note: houses says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A lad skipped around the houses in his street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' reads as a noun, the buildings the boy skipped round, but it is a verb: the words 'skipped round' contain the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedro is a boy's first name, Spanish for Peter, so it is one example of a boy.

clue.text: Second tout in court

parts.note: a runner is a tout who drums up business, for example for a bookmaker
to be up before the judge is to be in court

explanation.surface: A second ticket tout ends up facing a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads as an ordinal, the next tout, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The competitor who finishes in second place is the runner-up.

clue.text: That glen drawn extensively

indicators.note: drawn as in pulled out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A valley sketched in great detail by an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawn' suggests sketching, but it means pulled about, so the letters of THAT GLEN are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something at length is to do it fully and for a long time, thoroughly.

clue.text: Former PM, Brown, to touch down in a county bordering Scotland

parts.note: Lord North was British prime minister during the American War of Independence
umber is a brown earth pigment
to land is to touch down, as an aircraft does

explanation.surface: A former prime minister, Gordon Brown, lands in a border county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former PM, Brown' reads as Gordon Brown, but they are two pieces: Lord North, and the colour umber.
explanation.definitionFit: Northumberland is the English county in the far north-east whose boundary meets Scotland.

clue.text: Fruit and a soft Italian cheese? No thank you

parts.note: P (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letters for thanks are dropped from the cheese

parts.note: ricotta is a soft Italian whey cheese
TA is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: Offered fruit with a soft Italian cheese, someone politely declines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No thank you' reads as refusing the cheese, but it says take TA (British slang for thanks) out of RICOTTA, leaving RICOT.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit related to the plum and peach.

clue.text: Said about loud noise first, maybe

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for spoken goes round the noise

parts.note: oral means spoken, said aloud rather than written
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: Someone said a loud noise came first, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: First is an example of an ordinal number, one showing position in a series; 'maybe' signals the example.

clue.text: See head of gorgeous girl in mirror

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: Look at the beautiful girl's face reflected in a mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass, short for looking glass, is a mirror.

clue.text: 3's wife could, struggling alone with a net

definitions.note: the phrase completes what the rhyme says Jack Sprat's wife could do

indicators.note: struggling means writhing about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone's wife wrestles alone with a fishing net.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' points to the answer at 3-down, Jack Sprat: the rhyme says he could eat no fat and his wife could eat no lean.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme line completes 'his wife could' with the words about refusing meat without fat.

clue.text: Stand around fine Barbarian leaving game?

indicators.note: the word for stand goes around the next two pieces

parts.note: to stand someone a drink is to treat them, so a stand is a treat
sure, as a reply, means fine or okay
the Huns were barbarian invaders of the Roman Empire

explanation.surface: A fine Barbarian rugby player walks off and rounds on a stand.
explanation.walkthrough: The Barbarians are a famous invitational rugby team, which makes 'leaving game' look like a sports report.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasure hunt is a game where players follow clues to find a hidden prize; the question mark marks it as one kind of game.

clue.text: Even-tempered going round Italian fair

indicators.note: the word for calm wraps around the abbreviation for Italian

parts.note: an equable person is calm and even-tempered

explanation.surface: A calm Italian takes a turn on the fairground rides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair' reads as a funfair the Italian goes round, but it means just.
explanation.definitionFit: Equitable means just and impartial, treating everyone fairly.

clue.text: Leash may, unfortunately, for dog

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dog lead may, sadly, be needed for the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sealyham is a small white Welsh terrier breed, so it is one example of a dog.

clue.text: Carry weapons to support members

parts.note: to bear a weight is to support it
arms are members, limbs of the body

explanation.surface: People carry guns to back up the members of their group.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear arms is the set phrase for carrying firearms, as in the US Second Amendment.

clue.text: Charged ahead of varsity rower, perhaps in a vivid colour

indicators.note: the word for charged comes before the next piece

parts.note: electric means charged with electricity
a Blue is a sportsman who has represented Oxford or Cambridge, for example rowing in the Boat Race

explanation.surface: A tense university oarsman, perhaps dressed in a bright shade.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge, a Blue is someone who has competed for the university against the other, as rowers do in the Boat Race.
explanation.definitionFit: Electric blue is a brilliant, steely shade of light blue.

clue.text: Small or large, let it free

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: to free something is to loosen it, so these letters are let loose into a new order

explanation.surface: Whether a thing is small or big, just release it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small or large' looks like a single idea, but only 'Small' is the definition; 'large' gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Little is a plain synonym for small in size.

clue.text: County town originally producing wine

parts.note: Clare is a county in the west of Ireland

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A county town first made its name making wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret is the British name for red Bordeaux wine.

clue.text: Civic leader confused old army men

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: OR (other ranks) is the military abbreviation for ordinary soldiers, men as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: A town's leader is bewildered by veterans of the army.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lord Mayor is the ceremonial head of a major city council, such as London's.

clue.text: Saw bishop out of bed, having gone up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters read from bottom to top
out of means leaving, so the bishop's letter is removed

parts.note: a river bed is its bottom
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: Someone saw a bishop get out of bed and go upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' reads as a past tense, seeing the bishop, but it is the noun for an old saying. 'out of' takes B from BOTTOM to leave OTTOM, and 'having gone up' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a proverb or saying, and a motto is a short guiding maxim.

clue.text: Fabric wife put in drawer

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so the wife's letter goes within the drawer

parts.note: a till is the money drawer of a cash register

explanation.surface: A wife puts some cloth away in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawer' suggests furniture, but here it is the cash drawer of a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Twill is a cloth woven with a pattern of diagonal ridges, as in denim.

clue.text: Breathe badly? Medicinal drink's required

indicators.note: badly means done wrongly, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Struggling to breathe, someone needs a soothing remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A herb tea, an infusion of herbs, is often taken as a remedy for ailments.

clue.text: Judges arrives carrying grip

definitions.note: an arbiter is one who judges; read as Judge's, the 's is 'is', linking a singular definition

indicators.note: carrying means holding inside, so the abbreviation surrounds the grip

parts.note: ARR is the timetable abbreviation for arrives
a bite is a grip, as of a tyre or tool on a surface

explanation.surface: A judge turns up holding a firm grip on proceedings.
explanation.walkthrough: ARR is how railway timetables abbreviate arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter is a person who settles a dispute, someone with authority to decide.

clue.text: Lucky charm found in the old lady's bed

parts.note: an old lady is a mother, ma, so the old lady's is MA'S
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: A good-luck token turns up in Mum's bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object kept to bring a team good fortune.

clue.text: Sticking with her through a depression

indicators.note: through means passing within, so the word her sits inside the other letters

parts.note: a dent is a depression in a surface

explanation.surface: Someone stands by her through a bout of depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' reads as low mood, but it is a dent in a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Adherent as an adjective means clinging or attached, the literal sense of adhering.
